commentary:
The story this morning is energy giving back ground — and everything else breathing easier because of it. Brent dropped 3.1% to $104 and WTI slipped back below $100, retreating from multi-month highs after the IEA cut its demand estimate, warning of a "lost period" in global oil consumption as the Iran war drags on and the Strait of Hormuz stays shut through year-end. Reports that Gulf states are weighing a rare Hormuz meeting with Iran added a diplomatic glimmer. That took the heat off a market that had sold stocks and bonds for four straight sessions on the oil-driven yield surge: S&P and Nasdaq futures are up around half a percent, Treasuries found relief at the long end, and TTF gas eased 1.9%.

But don't confuse retreat with resolution — US retail diesel just topped $6 a gallon for the first time, a supply shock that feeds straight into inflation ahead of today's pivotal August CPI. That CPI print is the whole ballgame: traders want a clear signal on whether the Fed hikes next week, with the 10-year flirting with 5% and Treasury's $6bn operation failing to break the bond-market "fever," according to reports. ECB policymakers are opening the door to more hikes on energy risk, the BoJ is expected to move this month with 10-year JGBs near 3% — a global rate reset that pressures Treasury demand from Japan's $1.1tn holdings.

Watch the transmission: gold and silver eased as havens unwound; grains and soybean oil tracked energy lower, though record diesel is a direct cost shock for US agriculture; cocoa bucked the tape, up 3% on supply tightness. A hot CPI reprices SOFR strips and slams the long end — position accordingly.
